title: Count Pairs with given sum
directAnswer: Count the number of index pairs `(i, j)` with `i < j` and `arr[i] + arr[j] = target`. Walk once with a frequency map of values seen so far: for each `x`, add `freq[target − x]` to the running count (every earlier occurrence of the complement forms one pair with the current element), then increment `freq[x]`. O(n) time, O(n) space — and unlike Two Sum we add the frequency rather than returning on the first hit, because we want *all* pairs.

rules: Add `freq[target − x]` **before** inserting `x` — this counts the current element against every *earlier* complement, so each unordered pair is counted exactly once.
Store value → **count**, not value → index — you need the multiplicity, since duplicates create multiple pairs.
Don't return early: this is a counting problem, so accumulate over the whole array.
Use a count accumulator wide enough for the worst case — all-equal arrays give C(n,2) pairs, which can exceed int for large n.
Handle the complement equal to the current value naturally: the freq map already holds only *earlier* equal elements, so `x + x = target` duplicates are counted correctly without special casing.
whenToUse: Count (not just find) pairs/matches that sum or XOR to a target
Unsorted array, duplicates allowed, need multiplicity
You can phrase the question as 'how many earlier elements complete me?'
antiSignals: Array is sorted and you want O(1) space → two pointers counting pairs
You need the actual pairs/indices, not a count → collect them instead of tallying
You only need one pair → Two Sum's return-on-first-hit
Target relation isn't a simple complement (e.g. product) → adjust the lookup key
remember.takeaway: Counting pairs is Two Sum with two tweaks: keep a frequency *count* instead of an index, and *accumulate* matches instead of returning. Looking up the complement before inserting guarantees each pair is counted once.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you adapt the complement-lookup pattern from 'find one pair' to 'count all pairs' without double counting, and whether you reason about duplicates.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Double counting by scanning the whole map (counting both (i,j) and (j,i)), inserting before the lookup, or storing an index instead of a frequency so duplicates are undercounted.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Note that looking up before inserting makes the count 'pairs with an earlier element', which is exactly each unordered pair once — no division by two, no special case for equal halves.

problemStatement:
Given an array `arr` of `n` integers and an integer `target`, count the number of pairs of indices `(i, j)` with `i < j` such that `arr[i] + arr[j] = target`.

Return the count. Values may repeat and may be negative.
constraints: Pairs are unordered: (i, j) and (j, i) are the same pair
understanding: Tally how many unordered index pairs sum to target. Duplicates multiply the count: if value v appears p times and target − v appears q times (v ≠ target − v), that's p·q pairs; if v = target − v, it's C(p,2). The single-pass complement-frequency method produces this total without explicit casework.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are pairs ordered or unordered?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Unordered. (i, j) and (j, i) are the same pair, so each must be counted once — the before-insert lookup guarantees that.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the same element be used twice?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, i ≠ j. But two different indices holding the same value is a valid pair, e.g. arr = [3, 3], target = 6 → 1 pair.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can values be negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. The complement target − x works for negatives too; don't assume positivity.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we count or return the pairs?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Count. That's the key difference from Two Sum — we accumulate matches across the whole array instead of returning on the first.

examples.explanation: (1,5) at indices (0,1), (1,5) at (0,4), and (7,−1) at (2,3). The doubled 5 creates two pairs with the single 1.
Every pair of 1s sums to 2 → C(4,2) = 6.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Nested Pair Scan
approaches.whenToMention: State it first to define the count, then improve to a single pass.
hints: How many unordered pairs are there, and how would you test each one's sum?
Two nested loops with j > i so each pair is visited once.
Increment a counter whenever arr[i] + arr[j] == target.
approaches.complexityReasoning: n(n−1)/2 pairs, each summed and compared in O(1).
approaches.explanation:
Check every unordered pair directly. The outer loop fixes `i`; the inner loop runs `j` from `i + 1` to the end so each pair `{i, j}` is examined exactly once.

**Why `j = i + 1`.** Starting `j` past `i` avoids pairing an element with itself and avoids counting `{i, j}` twice (once as `(i, j)`, once as `(j, i)`). This is the same loop-invariant trick as in Two Sum.

**Why it's only a warm-up.** For `n = 10⁵`, ~5×10⁹ comparisons is far too slow. It establishes the definition of the count; the frequency map makes it linear.
approaches.insight: The `j = i + 1` bound is what makes the brute force count *unordered* pairs once. Keep that 'each pair once' framing — the optimal version reproduces it by only looking at earlier elements.

approaches.name: Frequency Map — One Pass (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want — adapt Two Sum's complement lookup to counting.
hints: For each element x, how many already-seen elements equal target − x? Each is one pair with x.
Keep a map of value → count of occurrences so far. Look up target − x before inserting x.
Add freq[target − x] to the answer, then bump freq[x]. One pass, all pairs counted once.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Single pass with O(1) average map operations; the map holds up to n distinct keys → O(n) time and space.
approaches.explanation:
Walk the array once, maintaining `freq`, a map from value to how many times it has appeared **so far**. For the current element `x`, the number of new pairs it completes is `freq[target − x]` — every earlier element equal to the complement pairs with `x`. Add that to the count, then record `x` by incrementing `freq[x]`.

**Why look up before inserting.** By querying `freq` *before* adding `x`, the map contains only elements at earlier indices. So each pair is counted exactly once, at the moment its *later* element is processed. No factor-of-two correction, no separate handling for the `x = target − x` case — equal earlier elements are already in the map with the right multiplicity.

**Why a frequency, not an index.** Two Sum stores value → index because it needs one witness. Here duplicates matter: if the complement appeared 3 times before, `x` forms 3 pairs. So we store value → *count*.

**Why accumulate, not return.** The task is a total, so we never short-circuit. The accumulator should be wide enough — an all-equal array gives `C(n,2)` pairs, which can overflow a 32-bit int for large `n` (use `long` in Java).
approaches.insight: This is the counting twin of Two Sum: same complement-lookup skeleton, but 'store index, return early' becomes 'store frequency, accumulate'. Recognizing that one-line-of-thought difference lets you reuse the pattern across find-vs-count variants (Subarray Sum Equals K is the prefix-sum version of this exact move).

dryRun.intro: freq holds counts of earlier elements. Add freq[target − x] before recording x.

code.python:
def count_pairs(arr: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    from collections import defaultdict
    freq: dict[int, int] = defaultdict(int)
    count = 0
    for x in arr:
        count += freq[target - x]
        freq[x] += 1
    return count

Record x's occurrence so later elements can pair with it.

python.explanation: defaultdict yields 0 for unseen complements; add the count of earlier matches.
Increment after the lookup so x only pairs with strictly earlier elements.

commonMistakes: Inserting into the frequency map before looking up the complement.
Counting both (i, j) and (j, i), doubling the answer.
Storing a single index instead of a count, undercounting duplicate values.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Insert before lookup (self-pair / double count)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If x is recorded before the complement lookup and 2x = target, x pairs with itself; more generally it shifts every count and breaks the 'each pair once' invariant.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Index instead of frequency
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Two Sum stores value → index because it needs one witness. Counting needs multiplicity: storing only the last index loses how many earlier complements exist.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
Map<Integer, Integer> lastIndex = new HashMap<>();
// ... if contains complement, count++;
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
// ... count += freq.getOrDefault(target - x, 0);

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Overflow on the count
commonMistakesDetailed.why: An all-equal array gives C(n,2) pairs ≈ n²/2, which overflows int for n around 10⁵.
